## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Inverse Problems and Imaging: Statistical and Stochastic Approaches
  Official title       Problèmes inverses et imagerie : approches statistiques et stochastiques
  Instructors          J. GARNIER (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 27 h (lectures 27 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com course description is written in French)
  Assessment           Projects (with a numerical implementation or purely theoretical), hand-in of a report and an oral presentation (master-mva.com, “Mode de validation”) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment) · weights not displayed
  Prerequisites        Probability, analysis (Fourier), linear algebra (master-mva.com, “Prè-requis”)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an M2 student with a good M1 in applied mathematics, physics or signal processing who wants to image a medium from the waves recorded by an array of sensors — an ultrasound probe, a network of seismometers, an antenna — and to know what noise allows and forbids.

**Empirical first**: in Code 1.10, 41 sensors record the echoes of two small reflectors with a measurement noise as strong as the signal in every entry of the data matrix. Yet the two largest singular values of that matrix stand clearly above the noise edge predicted by random matrix theory, and migration puts the first reflector at the right point to within a tenth of a wavelength (Code 3.12). In seismology, correlating weeks of ambient noise at two stations reveals the travel time between them without any controlled source; ch. 7 explains why.

The module studies multi-sensor imaging, as in ultrasound echography or seismic imaging, as a statistical problem. Waves carry information about a medium to an array; noise corrupts it; an imaging method must decide whether a target is present, where it is and what it is, with error rates that can be computed. Four mathematical tools organise the course: least squares and Bayesian regularisation, time reversal and the Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity, random matrix theory, and the spectral theory of stationary processes.

It shares random matrices with [Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html), hypothesis testing with [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html), Bayesian inverse problems with [Learning Physical Phenomena: Metamodelling and Uncertainty Quantification](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html), and learned reconstruction with [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Formulate an imaging problem as detection, localisation, characterisation or identification, and write the corresponding statistical model.
-   Compute Green's functions of the wave equation and the multistatic response matrix of point reflectors in the Born approximation.
-   Solve a linear inverse problem by least squares, diagnose its ill-posedness from the singular values, and regularise it by truncation or Tikhonov's method.
-   Read Tikhonov regularisation as Bayesian inference, and compute posterior means and covariances.
-   Derive the resolution of time-reversal and migration imaging from the Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity.
-   Use the Marchenko–Pastur law and the spiked-model phase transition to predict the singular values of noisy response matrices.
-   Build detection tests with a prescribed false-alarm rate, compute their power, and estimate the position and strength of a detected reflector.
-   Compute the power spectral density of a stationary process and the statistical fluctuations of empirical correlations.
-   Retrieve travel times and Green's functions from cross-correlations of ambient noise, and image with them.
-   Implement every method above in a few lines of NumPy and check it against the theory.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: probability, analysis (Fourier) and linear algebra. The module is a second-semester Modelling course of the Santé track.

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (Gaussian vectors, likelihood, tests), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (SVD, least squares, Fourier) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html).
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (ridge regression is Tikhonov regularisation), [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Bayesian computation), [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html) (stationary processes), [Statistical Learning for Scientific Imaging and Physical Measurements: Geosciences](../s1-ml-geosciences/index.html), [Medical Image Analysis](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html).
-   **Related courses of the same semester** — [Large Random Matrices](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html), [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html), [Learning Physical Phenomena](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html), [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html), [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html), [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html).
-   **Afterwards** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html): wave imaging, ultrasound and seismology laboratories host many MVA interns.

### Course outline

-   **Review** — Fourier transform and correlation, SVD, Weyl and Eckart–Young, complex Gaussian vectors and conditioning.
-   **Imaging problems, waves and noise** — the four imaging tasks, the wave and Helmholtz equations, Green's functions, the Born approximation, the multistatic response matrix, noise models.
-   **Least squares, ill-posedness and Bayesian regularisation** — pseudo-inverse and Gauss–Markov, noise amplification, spectral filters, the discrepancy principle, Gaussian posteriors.
-   **Time-reversal imaging** — migration as the adjoint, the time-reversal experiment, the Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity, resolution formulas, signal-to-noise ratio, DORT and MUSIC.
-   **Random matrix theory** — the Marchenko–Pastur law by the moment method, the edge and Tracy–Widom, the spiked model and its phase transition.
-   **Detection tests** — Neyman–Pearson, generalised likelihood ratios, thresholds and power, then localisation and characterisation of what was detected.
-   **Stationary random processes** — Wiener–Khinchin, filtering, the variance of empirical correlations, the periodogram.
-   **Ambient noise cross-correlations** — Green's function retrieval, directivity of the sources, travel times, passive imaging.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — imaging in complex media, high-dimensional detection, learned reconstruction, noise-based monitoring (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1: the SVD, Eckart–Young and complex Gaussian vectors return in every later chapter.
-   Keep one geometry in mind throughout: a linear array of sensors facing a few point reflectors. Codes 1.10 and 3.12, and Exercise 12, all use it.
-   After each session, run the chapter's code and change one parameter (noise level, number of sensors, bandwidth); predict the effect before running it.
-   Do the exercises of the *Practice* column within the week; the ★★ exercises are close to the written-exam questions.
-   The Python environment is NumPy and SciPy on a CPU; every code block runs in a few seconds on a laptop.

## 0. Review: Fourier analysis, singular values and Gaussian vectors {#ch0}

Three M1 tools carry the whole module. The Fourier transform turns the wave equation into the Helmholtz equation and correlations into products; the singular value decomposition organises least squares, imaging and detection; complex Gaussian vectors model the noise on array data.

This chapter fixes the conventions and proves the facts used later. The refreshers on [linear algebra](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and [probability](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) give more background.

### Fourier transform and correlations

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Fourier transform in time]{.tag} For an integrable signal $f(t)$ we use the convention of wave propagation:
$$
\hat f(\omega) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt, \qquad f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \hat f(\omega)\, e^{-i\omega t}\, d\omega .
$$

A real signal has central angular frequency $\omega_0$ and bandwidth $B$ (in hertz) when $\hat f(\omega)$ vanishes outside the two bands where $\big||\omega| - \omega_0\big| \leq \pi B$.
:::

With this sign, $\partial_t f$ has transform $-i\omega \hat f$, so a time derivative becomes a multiplication.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Convolution, correlation, Plancherel]{.tag} For real square-integrable signals $f$ and $g$, define the convolution and the cross-correlation
$$
(f * g)(t) = \int f(s)\, g(t - s)\, ds, \qquad (f \star g)(\tau) = \int f(t)\, g(t + \tau)\, dt .
$$

Their Fourier transforms are
$$
\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\, \hat g, \qquad \widehat{f \star g} = \overline{\hat f}\, \hat g, \qquad \int f(t)^2\, dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int |\hat f(\omega)|^2\, d\omega .
$$

::: proof
For the correlation, exchange the integrals and substitute $s = t + \tau$:
$$
\int e^{i\omega \tau} \int f(t)\, g(t+\tau)\, dt\, d\tau = \int f(t)\, e^{-i\omega t} dt \int g(s)\, e^{i\omega s} ds .
$$

The first factor is the conjugate of the transform of $f$ because $f$ is real. The convolution is the same computation, and Plancherel's identity is the correlation formula at $\tau = 0$ with $g = f$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The correlation formula is the heart of ch. 6 and ch. 7: correlating two recordings multiplies one spectrum by the conjugate of the other, which cancels the common phase of the source.

### Singular values

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Singular value decomposition]{.tag} Every complex matrix $M \in \mathbb{C}^{N \times M}$ factorises as
$$
M = \sum_{j=1}^{\min(N, M)} \sigma_j\, u_j v_j^* ,
$$
with orthonormal left vectors $u_j$, orthonormal right vectors $v_j$, and singular values $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \dots \geq 0$.

The operator norm is $\|M\| = \sigma_1$ and the Frobenius norm satisfies $\|M\|_F^2 = \sum_j \sigma_j^2$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.4 — Weyl's perturbation bound]{.tag} For matrices $M$ and $E$ of the same size and every index $j$,
$$
|\sigma_j(M + E) - \sigma_j(M)| \leq \|E\| .
$$

::: proof
The min–max characterisation of singular values states that $\sigma_j(M)$ is the maximum, over subspaces $V$ of dimension $j$, of the minimum of $\|Mx\|$ over unit vectors $x \in V$.

For every unit $x$, the triangle inequality gives $\|(M+E)x\| \geq \|Mx\| - \|E\|$. Taking the minimum over $V$ and then the maximum over $V$ gives $\sigma_j(M+E) \geq \sigma_j(M) - \|E\|$.

Exchanging the roles of $M$ and $M + E$ gives the other inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Weyl's bound says that noise of norm $\|E\|$ cannot move a singular value by more than $\|E\|$. Ch. 4 shows that for random noise this bound is pessimistic, and computes the exact displacement.

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Eckart–Young, rank-one case]{.tag} For every matrix $M$,
$$
\min_{\mathrm{rank}(B) \leq 1} \|M - B\|_F^2 = \|M\|_F^2 - \sigma_1(M)^2 ,
$$
and the minimum is attained at $B = \sigma_1 u_1 v_1^*$.

::: proof
Write $B = c\, u v^*$ with unit vectors $u, v$ and $c \in \mathbb{C}$. Expanding the square,
$$
\|M - c\, u v^*\|_F^2 = \|M\|_F^2 - 2\, \mathrm{Re}\big(\bar c\, u^* M v\big) + |c|^2 .
$$

For fixed $u, v$ the minimum in $c$ is reached at $c = u^* M v$ and equals the first term minus $|u^* M v|^2$.

The maximum of $|u^* M v|$ over unit vectors is $\sigma_1$, reached at $u_1, v_1$; this is the variational definition of $\sigma_1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The general statement replaces $\sigma_1^2$ by the sum of the $r$ largest $\sigma_j^2$ for rank at most $r$; its proof uses a refined form of Weyl's inequality (see Horn and Johnson, *Matrix Analysis*).
::::

### Complex Gaussian vectors

At a fixed frequency, sensor data are complex numbers, and their noise is modelled by circularly symmetric complex Gaussian variables.

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Circular complex Gaussian]{.tag} A random variable $Z = X + iY$ is $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2/2)$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}|Z|^2 = \sigma^2, \qquad \mathbb{E} Z^2 = 0 .
$$

A random vector $Z \in \mathbb{C}^N$ is $\mathcal{CN}(0, \Gamma)$ when every linear form $a^* Z$ is $\mathcal{CN}(0, a^* \Gamma a)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Three facts about complex Gaussian noise]{.tag} Let $W$ be an $N \times N$ matrix with independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ entries.

1.  For deterministic unit vectors $u, v$, the projection $u^* W v$ is $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$.
2.  If $Z$ is $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$, then $|Z|^2$ is exponential with mean $\sigma^2$.
3.  For deterministic unitary matrices $U, V$, the matrix $U W V^*$ has the same law as $W$.

::: proof
1\. The projection is a linear combination of independent circular Gaussians with coefficients $\bar u_n v_m$, whose squared moduli sum to one.

2\. The variable $2|Z|^2 / \sigma^2$ is a chi-square with two degrees of freedom, which is exponential with mean 2.

3\. The entries of $U W V^*$ are jointly circular Gaussian. Their covariances follow from those of $W$ and the unitarity of $U$ and $V$, and coincide with those of $W$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Unitary invariance (fact 3) is why the singular values of pure noise carry no information about any direction: ch. 4 and ch. 5 rest on it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Conditioning a Gaussian vector]{.tag} Let $(Z_1, Z_2)$ be a real Gaussian vector with zero mean and covariance blocks $\Sigma_{11}, \Sigma_{12}, \Sigma_{22}$, with $\Sigma_{22}$ invertible. The law of $Z_1$ given $Z_2 = z_2$ is Gaussian, with
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z_1 \mid Z_2 = z_2] = \Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} z_2, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(Z_1 \mid Z_2) = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} \Sigma_{21} .
$$

::: proof
Set $V = Z_1 - \Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} Z_2$. Its covariance with $Z_2$ is $\Sigma_{12} - \Sigma_{12} = 0$.

The pair $(V, Z_2)$ is Gaussian, so $V$ is independent of $Z_2$.

Given $Z_2 = z_2$, $Z_1$ is $V$ plus the constant $\Sigma_{12} \Sigma_{22}^{-1} z_2$, and the covariance of $V$ is the stated matrix. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   With the convention of Definition 0.1, correlating two signals multiplies the conjugate of one spectrum by the other (Proposition 0.2).
-   A perturbation of norm $\|E\|$ moves every singular value by at most $\|E\|$ (Theorem 0.4).
-   The best rank-one approximation in Frobenius norm is the leading singular triplet (Theorem 0.5).
-   Matrices with independent circular Gaussian entries are unitarily invariant, and their projections on fixed vectors are again circular Gaussian (Proposition 0.7).
-   Gaussian conditioning gives a mean linear in the data and a covariance independent of the data (Proposition 0.8).
:::

## 1. Imaging problems, waves and noise {#ch1}

Before computing any image, one must say what is measured, how waves carry information about the medium to the sensors, and what corrupts that information. This chapter sets up the forward model used in the whole module: point reflectors probed by an array, in the Born approximation, with additive noise.

### The four imaging tasks

An array of $N$ sensors at positions $x_1, \dots, x_N$ emits waves and records the echoes, or simply listens. The data $D$ are noisy, and the questions asked about the medium form a hierarchy.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Detection, localisation, characterisation, identification]{.tag}

-   **Detection**: decide between the hypothesis $H_0$ (the data contain only noise) and $H_1$ (a target is present), with a controlled probability of false alarm.
-   **Localisation**: estimate the position $z$ of a target known to be present.
-   **Characterisation**: estimate parameters of the target, such as its reflectivity, its size or its shape.
-   **Identification**: decide which element of a dictionary of known targets is present.
:::

Each task needs more information than the previous one, hence a higher signal-to-noise ratio. A reflector can be detected and not located, or located and not characterised; ch. 5 makes these thresholds quantitative.

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Two imaging regimes]{.tag}

-   **Ultrasound echography.** In soft tissue the speed of sound is about 1540 m/s; at a central frequency of 5 MHz the wavelength is
    $$
    \lambda = c_0 / f_0 \approx 0.31 \text{ mm}.
    $$
    A probe of a few centimetres images organs a few centimetres deep.
-   **Seismic imaging.** With speeds of a few km/s and frequencies of a few tens of hertz, wavelengths range from tens to hundreds of metres, and arrays of geophones span kilometres.
-   In both cases the array aperture is tens or hundreds of wavelengths, and the targets are a few wavelengths to hundreds of wavelengths away.
:::

### Waves and Green's functions

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Wave and Helmholtz equations]{.tag} A scalar wave $u(t, x)$ in a medium of speed $c(x)$ excited by a source term $F(t, x)$ solves
$$
\frac{1}{c(x)^2}\, \partial_t^2 u - \Delta u = F .
$$

Taking the Fourier transform in time (Definition 0.1) gives the Helmholtz equation
$$
\Delta \hat u + \frac{\omega^2}{c(x)^2}\, \hat u = -\hat F .
$$

In a homogeneous medium of speed $c_0$, the wavenumber is $k = \omega / c_0$ and the wavelength is $\lambda = 2\pi / k$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Green's functions of a homogeneous medium]{.tag} The outgoing Green's function solves $\Delta \hat G + k^2 \hat G = -\delta(x - y)$ with the Sommerfeld radiation condition. In three dimensions,
$$
\hat G(\omega, x, y) = \frac{e^{i k |x - y|}}{4\pi |x - y|}, \qquad G(t, x, y) = \frac{\delta\big(t - |x - y| / c_0\big)}{4\pi |x - y|} .
$$

In two dimensions, with the Hankel function of the first kind,
$$
\hat G(\omega, x, y) = \frac{i}{4} H_0^{(1)}(k |x - y|) \approx \frac{i}{4} \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi k |x - y|}}\; e^{i (k |x - y| - \pi/4)} \quad (k|x-y| \gg 1) .
$$

::: proof
Three dimensions, with $r = |x - y|$. For a radial function, $\Delta \hat G = r^{-1} (r \hat G)''$. Here $r \hat G = e^{ikr}/4\pi$ has second derivative $-k^2 r \hat G$, so $\Delta \hat G + k^2 \hat G = 0$ for $r > 0$.

Near $r = 0$, $\hat G$ behaves like $1/(4\pi r)$. The flux of its gradient through a sphere of radius $\varepsilon$ tends to $-1$, which is the weak form of $-\delta$:
$$
4\pi\varepsilon^2\, \partial_r \hat G(\varepsilon) = (ik\varepsilon - 1)\, e^{ik\varepsilon} \longrightarrow -1 .
$$

The radiation condition holds because $\partial_r \hat G - ik \hat G = -\hat G / r$. The inverse Fourier transform of $e^{i\omega r/c_0}$ is $\delta(t - r/c_0)$, which gives the time-domain formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The time-domain formula says that an impulse emitted at $y$ reaches $x$ after the travel time $|x - y|/c_0$, with amplitude decaying like the inverse distance. Green's functions are also symmetric, $\hat G(\omega, x, y) = \hat G(\omega, y, x)$, even in heterogeneous media: this is the reciprocity principle.

### Reflectors and the multistatic response matrix

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Born approximation]{.tag} Let the medium be a homogeneous background perturbed by a reflectivity $\nu$ of compact support:
$$
\frac{1}{c(x)^2} = \frac{1 + \nu(x)}{c_0^2} .
$$

The field emitted by a point source at $y$ is $\hat G(x, y) + \hat u_s(x)$, and the scattered field solves the Lippmann–Schwinger equation
$$
\hat u_s(x) = k^2 \int \nu(z)\, \hat G(x, z)\, \big[\hat G(z, y) + \hat u_s(z)\big]\, dz .
$$

The Born approximation drops $\hat u_s$ inside the integral. For a small reflector at $z_r$ with $\rho_r = \int \nu$, it gives
$$
\hat u_s(x) \approx k^2 \rho_r\, \hat G(x, z_r)\, \hat G(z_r, y) .
$$

::: proof
Subtracting the equation of $\hat G(\cdot, y)$ from the Helmholtz equation of the total field gives
$$
\Delta \hat u_s + k^2 \hat u_s = -k^2 \nu \big(\hat G(\cdot, y) + \hat u_s\big) .
$$

The right-hand side is a source term, so convolving it with the Green's function gives the Lippmann–Schwinger equation. Dropping $\hat u_s$ on the right is the first-order term in $\nu$. When $\nu$ is concentrated near $z_r$, the integral reduces to the value of the integrand at $z_r$ times $\int \nu$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Born approximation neglects multiple scattering. It is accurate when the reflectivity is weak and the reflectors are small compared with the wavelength, which is the regime of this module.

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Illumination vector and multistatic response matrix]{.tag} The illumination vector of a point $z$ collects the Green's functions from the sensors:
$$
g(z) = \big(\hat G(\omega, x_1, z), \dots, \hat G(\omega, x_N, z)\big)^\top \in \mathbb{C}^N .
$$

The multistatic response (MSR) matrix $A(\omega) \in \mathbb{C}^{N \times N}$ has entry $A_{nm}$ equal to the scattered field recorded at $x_n$ when $x_m$ emits a unit point source.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Structure of the MSR matrix]{.tag} In the Born approximation, $R$ point reflectors at $z_1, \dots, z_R$ with reflectivities $\rho_1, \dots, \rho_R$ produce
$$
A = k^2 \sum_{r=1}^{R} \rho_r\, g(z_r)\, g(z_r)^\top .
$$

The matrix is complex symmetric, and its rank is $R$ when the vectors $g(z_r)$ are linearly independent. For a single reflector, its only nonzero singular value is
$$
\sigma_1 = |\rho_1|\, k^2\, \|g(z_1)\|^2 ,
$$
with left vector $g(z_1)/\|g(z_1)\|$ and right vector $\overline{g(z_1)}/\|g(z_1)\|$, up to a phase.

::: proof
Apply Proposition 1.5 with $y = x_m$ and $x = x_n$, and sum over the reflectors, which the Born approximation treats independently. Each term is a rank-one symmetric matrix.

For one reflector, write $g g^\top = \|g\|^2\, (g/\|g\|)\, (\bar g/\|g\|)^*$, which is a singular value decomposition up to the phase of $\rho_1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In the time domain, in three dimensions, the entry $A_{nm}(t)$ for a pulse $f$ is an echo arriving at the round-trip travel time $T_{nm}$:
$$
A_{nm}(t) = -\frac{\rho_1}{16\pi^2 c_0^2\, |x_n - z_1|\, |z_1 - x_m|}\; f''\big(t - T_{nm}\big), \qquad T_{nm} = \frac{|x_n - z_1| + |z_1 - x_m|}{c_0} .
$$

### Noise models

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Three kinds of noise]{.tag}

-   **Additive measurement noise.** At each frequency the measured matrix is $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = A + W$, where $W$ has independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ entries. It models the electronic noise of the sensors; ch. 6 explains why the Fourier coefficients of a stationary noise are nearly independent circular Gaussians.
-   **Clutter.** The background medium itself fluctuates, and many small heterogeneities send random echoes, the speckle of echography. This noise is generated by the probing wave, so it does not average out over repeated shots.
-   **Ambient noise.** Uncontrolled sources, such as ocean waves or traffic, emit stationary random signals. They are a nuisance for active imaging and a resource for passive imaging (ch. 7).
:::

This module mostly uses the first model, which allows exact computations; the research chapter returns to clutter.

::: ex
[Example 1.9 — Weak entries, strong matrix]{.tag} In Code 1.10, 41 sensors with half-wavelength spacing face two reflectors about 30 wavelengths away.

-   The typical modulus of an entry of $A$ is 0.0094, and the noise level is $\sigma = 0.01$: each entry has a signal-to-noise ratio below one.
-   The two nonzero singular values of $A$ are 0.335 and 0.188, while the singular values of pure noise stay below about $2\sigma\sqrt N = 0.128$ (ch. 4).
-   The matrix as a whole therefore carries a clear signal: coherence across the $N^2$ entries beats the noise of each entry.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import hankel1

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
lam = 1.0; k = 2 * np.pi / lam                 # lengths in wavelengths
N = 41
xs = np.stack([(np.arange(N) - 20) * lam / 2, np.zeros(N)], axis=1)   # array, aperture 20 lambda

def G(x, z):
    """2D outgoing Green's function (i/4) H0^(1)(k|x - z|)."""
    return 0.25j * hankel1(0, k * np.linalg.norm(x - z, axis=-1))

refl = [(np.array([-2.0, 30.0]), 1.0), (np.array([3.0, 32.0]), 0.6)]
A = sum(rho * k**2 * np.outer(G(xs, z), G(xs, z)) for z, rho in refl)   # Born MSR matrix
sigma = 0.01
W = sigma * (rng.standard_normal((N, N)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((N, N))) / np.sqrt(2)
s_clean = np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)
s_noisy = np.linalg.svd(A + W, compute_uv=False)
print("typical |A_nm|        :", np.round(np.median(np.abs(A)), 4))
print("clean singular values :", np.round(s_clean[:4], 4))
print("noisy singular values :", np.round(s_noisy[:4], 4))
print("noise edge 2 sigma sqrt(N):", np.round(2 * sigma * np.sqrt(N), 4))
```

::: ex
[Code 1.10 — What the code shows]{.tag} The clean matrix has exactly two nonzero singular values, 0.3353 and 0.1876, as Proposition 1.7 predicts for two reflectors.

With noise, they become 0.345 and 0.194, and the next ones, 0.116 and 0.112, belong to the noise bulk, below the edge 0.128. The upward shift of the two signal values is not a coincidence: ch. 4 predicts it.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   Imaging asks four questions of increasing difficulty: detection, localisation, characterisation, identification (Definition 1.1).
-   The Green's function of a homogeneous medium is an outgoing spherical wave, a delayed impulse in time (Proposition 1.4).
-   In the Born approximation, point reflectors make the MSR matrix a sum of rank-one terms built on illumination vectors (Proposition 1.7).
-   Measurement noise is modelled by independent circular Gaussian entries; clutter and ambient noise are the two other sources of randomness (Definition 1.8).
:::

## 2. Least squares, ill-posedness and Bayesian regularisation {#ch2}

Most imaging problems, once linearised, read $y = Kx + w$: unknown parameters $x$, a known forward operator $K$, noisy data $y$. This chapter asks when least squares can invert $K$, why it fails for imaging operators, and how regularisation and Bayesian priors restore stability.

Throughout, $K \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times P}$ has the singular value decomposition $K = \sum_j s_j u_j v_j^*$, with non-increasing $s_j$. The noise $w$ has mean zero and covariance $\sigma^2 I$.

We write $s_j$ for the singular values of $K$ to keep $\sigma$ for the noise.

### Least squares

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — Normal equations and pseudo-inverse]{.tag} The minimisers of $\|Kx - y\|^2$ are the solutions of the normal equations $K^* K x = K^* y$. Among them, the one of minimal norm is
$$
x^\dagger = K^\dagger y = \sum_{j : s_j > 0} \frac{u_j^* y}{s_j}\, v_j .
$$

::: proof
Complete $(u_j)$ and $(v_j)$ into orthonormal bases. In these bases, with $r$ the rank of $K$,
$$
\|Kx - y\|^2 = \sum_{j \leq r} \big|s_j\, v_j^* x - u_j^* y\big|^2 + \sum_{j > r} |u_j^* y|^2 .
$$

The minimisers are exactly the $x$ with $v_j^* x = u_j^* y / s_j$ for $j \leq r$, which is the normal equation written in the same bases. The other coordinates of $x$ are free, and setting them to zero minimises the norm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Gauss–Markov]{.tag} Let $K$ be injective. The least-squares estimator $\hat x = K^\dagger y$ is unbiased, with covariance $\sigma^2 (K^* K)^{-1}$, and every linear unbiased estimator $Ly$ satisfies
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Ly) \succeq \sigma^2 (K^* K)^{-1} .
$$

::: proof
Unbiasedness for every $x$ means $LK = I$. Write $L = K^\dagger + D$; then $DK = 0$.

The covariance of $Ly$ is $\sigma^2 L L^*$. The cross term vanishes because
$$
K^\dagger D^* = (K^* K)^{-1} (DK)^* = 0 .
$$

Hence $\mathrm{Cov}(Ly) = \sigma^2 (K^* K)^{-1} + \sigma^2 D D^*$, and the last term is positive semi-definite. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The mean squared error of least squares follows from the covariance:
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|\hat x - x\|^2 = \sigma^2\, \mathrm{tr}\, (K^* K)^{-1} = \sigma^2 \sum_j \frac{1}{s_j^2} .
$$

The best unbiased estimator can thus be useless: one tiny singular value suffices to ruin it.

### Ill-posedness

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Well-posed problem (Hadamard)]{.tag} The problem of finding $x$ from $y = Kx$ is well posed when a solution exists for every $y$, is unique, and depends continuously on $y$. Otherwise it is ill posed.
:::

In infinite dimension, a compact operator, such as a smoothing integral operator, has singular values accumulating at zero, so its inverse is unbounded. After discretisation the inverse exists but its norm is huge, and the problem stays ill posed in a quantitative sense.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Noise amplification]{.tag} Let $K$ be invertible with condition number $\kappa = s_1 / s_P$.

1.  A perturbation $\delta y$ of the data causes an error $\delta x = K^{-1} \delta y$ with
    $$
    \frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \leq \kappa\, \frac{\|\delta y\|}{\|y\|} .
    $$
2.  With noise of covariance $\sigma^2 I$, the error of $K^{-1} y$ along $v_j$ is $u_j^* w / s_j$, of variance $\sigma^2 / s_j^2$.

::: proof
1\. Combine $\|\delta x\| \leq \|\delta y\| / s_P$ with $\|y\| \leq s_1 \|x\|$.

2\. Expand $K^{-1} w$ in the singular bases: its coordinate along $v_j$ is $u_j^* w / s_j$, and $u_j^* w$ has variance $\sigma^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The data coefficients $u_j^* y$ split into a signal part, $s_j v_j^* x$, which decays with $j$, and a noise part of constant size $\sigma$. Beyond the index where $s_j$ falls below the noise, the coefficients are pure noise; Picard's condition says that a meaningful solution needs the signal coefficients to decay faster than $s_j$.

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Gaussian blur]{.tag} In Code 2.13, a signal of 200 samples on $[0, 1]$ is blurred by a Gaussian kernel of width 0.03, and a noise of level $\sigma = 10^{-3}$ is added.

-   The condition number of $K$ is $6.2 \cdot 10^{16}$.
-   Least squares returns a relative error of $2.5 \cdot 10^{13}$: the reconstruction is pure amplified noise.
:::

### Regularisation by spectral filtering

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Spectral filters]{.tag} A regularised solution damps the small singular values by a filter $\varphi_\alpha$ with values in $[0, 1]$:
$$
x_\alpha = \sum_j \varphi_\alpha(s_j)\, \frac{u_j^* y}{s_j}\, v_j .
$$

-   **Truncated SVD (TSVD)** keeps the coefficients with $s_j^2 \geq \alpha$: $\varphi_\alpha(s) = \mathbb{1}[s^2 \geq \alpha]$.
-   **Tikhonov** damps them smoothly: $\varphi_\alpha(s) = s^2 / (s^2 + \alpha)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Variational form of Tikhonov regularisation]{.tag} For $\alpha > 0$, the Tikhonov solution is the unique minimiser
$$
x_\alpha = \arg\min_x \|Kx - y\|^2 + \alpha \|x\|^2 = (K^* K + \alpha I)^{-1} K^* y .
$$

::: proof
The functional is strictly convex, and its gradient vanishes when $(K^* K + \alpha I) x = K^* y$, a system with an invertible matrix.

In the basis $(v_j)$ the matrix is diagonal with entries $s_j^2 + \alpha$, and $K^* y$ has coordinates $s_j\, u_j^* y$. The solution has coordinates $s_j\, u_j^* y / (s_j^2 + \alpha)$, which is the Tikhonov filter. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.8 — Bias–variance decomposition]{.tag} With $\varphi_j = \varphi_\alpha(s_j)$, the mean squared error of a filtered solution is
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|x_\alpha - x\|^2 = \underbrace{\sum_j (1 - \varphi_j)^2\, |v_j^* x|^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\sigma^2 \sum_j \frac{\varphi_j^2}{s_j^2}}_{\text{variance}} .
$$

For Tikhonov, each variance term is at most $\sigma^2 / (4\alpha)$, whatever the size of $s_j$.

::: proof
The coordinate of $x_\alpha - x$ along $v_j$ is
$$
(\varphi_j - 1)\, v_j^* x + \varphi_j\, \frac{u_j^* w}{s_j} .
$$

The second term has mean zero and variance $\sigma^2 \varphi_j^2 / s_j^2$, so the cross term vanishes in expectation. Summing over $j$ gives the formula.

For Tikhonov, $\varphi_j^2 / s_j^2 = s_j^2 / (s_j^2 + \alpha)^2$, and $(s^2 + \alpha)^2 \geq 4 \alpha s^2$ by the arithmetic–geometric inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Increasing $\alpha$ trades variance for bias; the best $\alpha$ depends on the unknown $x$, so it must be chosen from the data.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Discrepancy principle (Morozov)]{.tag} For Tikhonov regularisation, the residual $r(\alpha) = \|K x_\alpha - y\|$ is continuous and non-decreasing in $\alpha$.

At $\alpha = 0$ it equals the norm of the component of $y$ orthogonal to the range of $K$, and it tends to $\|y\|$ as $\alpha \to \infty$.

Hence, if the target lies between these two values, there is an $\alpha$ such that
$$
\|K x_\alpha - y\| = \tau\, \sigma \sqrt{M}, \qquad \tau \geq 1 .
$$

::: proof
In the singular bases, with $P_\perp$ the projection onto the orthogonal of the range,
$$
r(\alpha)^2 = \sum_j \Big(\frac{\alpha}{s_j^2 + \alpha}\Big)^2 |u_j^* y|^2 + \|P_\perp y\|^2 .
$$

Each term is continuous and non-decreasing in $\alpha$, with the stated limits; the intermediate value theorem concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The rationale is that $\mathbb{E}\|w\|^2 = M\sigma^2$: fitting the data more closely than the noise level means fitting the noise. Other rules, such as the L-curve and generalised cross-validation, do not need $\sigma$.

### Bayesian analysis

The Bayesian approach treats $x$ as random, with a prior law that encodes what is known before the measurement. Regularisation then appears as a consequence rather than a recipe. We state the real case; the circular complex case is identical with conjugate transposes.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.10 — Gaussian posterior]{.tag} Let $x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Gamma)$ and $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ be independent, and $y = Kx + w$. Given $y$, $x$ is Gaussian with mean and covariance
$$
m = \big(K^\top K + \sigma^2 \Gamma^{-1}\big)^{-1} K^\top y, \qquad C = \Big(\frac{K^\top K}{\sigma^2} + \Gamma^{-1}\Big)^{-1} .
$$

::: proof
The vector $(x, y)$ is Gaussian with $\mathrm{Cov}(x, y) = \Gamma K^\top$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(y) = K \Gamma K^\top + \sigma^2 I$. Proposition 0.8 gives
$$
m = \Gamma K^\top (K \Gamma K^\top + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad C = \Gamma - \Gamma K^\top (K \Gamma K^\top + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} K \Gamma .
$$

The identity
$$
(K^\top K + \sigma^2 \Gamma^{-1})\, \Gamma K^\top = K^\top (K \Gamma K^\top + \sigma^2 I)
$$
turns the first formula into the stated one. The Woodbury identity does the same for $C$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 2.11 — Tikhonov is a MAP estimator]{.tag} With the white prior $\Gamma = \gamma^2 I$, the posterior mean is the Tikhonov solution:

::: key
[Key result — regularisation from a prior]{.tag}
$$
m = (K^\top K + \alpha I)^{-1} K^\top y, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma^2} = \frac{\text{noise variance}}{\text{prior variance}} .
$$
:::

Since the posterior is Gaussian, its mean is also its mode, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. Indeed, minus the log-posterior is, up to a constant,
$$
\frac{\|Kx - y\|^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\|x\|^2}{2\gamma^2} .
$$
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.12 — The posterior mean minimises the Bayes risk]{.tag} Among all estimators $\hat x(y)$, measurable functions of the data, the posterior mean minimises $\mathbb{E}\|\hat x(y) - x\|^2$, and its risk is $\mathrm{tr}\, C$.

::: proof
Conditionally on $y$, with $m = m(y)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat x(y) - x\|^2 \mid y\big] = \|\hat x(y) - m\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\, C .
$$

The first term vanishes only for $\hat x = m$; taking the expectation over $y$ concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The posterior covariance quantifies the uncertainty. Along $v_j$, the posterior standard deviation is close to $\sigma / s_j$ when $s_j^2 \gg \alpha$, and close to $\gamma$ when $s_j^2 \ll \alpha$: the data inform the first directions, the prior alone the others.

Non-Gaussian priors change the picture. A Laplace prior gives an $\ell_1$-penalised MAP, which favours sparse reflectivities; the posterior is then no longer Gaussian and is explored by Markov chain Monte Carlo, as in [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html). The hyperparameters $\sigma^2$ and $\gamma^2$ can be estimated by maximising the marginal likelihood of $y$, which is $\mathcal{N}(0, K \Gamma K^\top + \sigma^2 I)$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 200
t = np.linspace(0, 1, n)
K = np.exp(-(t[:, None] - t[None, :])**2 / (2 * 0.03**2))       # Gaussian blur
K /= K.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
x_true = (np.abs(t - 0.3) < 0.08) + 0.6 * np.exp(-((t - 0.7) / 0.05)**2)
sigma = 1e-3
y = K @ x_true + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(K)
c = U.T @ y
err = lambda x: np.linalg.norm(x - x_true) / np.linalg.norm(x_true)
print(f"condition number {s[0] / s[-1]:.1e}; least squares rel. error {err(Vt.T @ (c / s)):.1e}")

def tikhonov(alpha):
    return Vt.T @ (s / (s**2 + alpha) * c)

# Morozov discrepancy principle: residual = sqrt(n) * sigma
alphas = np.logspace(-10, 0, 201)
res = np.array([np.linalg.norm(K @ tikhonov(a) - y) for a in alphas])
a_mor = alphas[np.argmin(np.abs(res - np.sqrt(n) * sigma))]
errs = np.array([err(tikhonov(a)) for a in alphas])
print(f"Tikhonov, Morozov alpha={a_mor:.1e}: rel. error {err(tikhonov(a_mor)):.3f}")
print(f"Tikhonov, oracle  alpha={alphas[errs.argmin()]:.1e}: rel. error {errs.min():.3f}")
for r in [10, 20, 40]:
    print(f"TSVD r={r:2d}: rel. error {err(Vt[:r].T @ (c[:r] / s[:r])):.3f}")

# Bayesian reading: prior N(0, gamma^2 I) with gamma^2 = sigma^2 / alpha
gamma = sigma / np.sqrt(a_mor)
post_sd = 1 / np.sqrt(s**2 / sigma**2 + 1 / gamma**2)   # posterior s.d. along each v_j
print(f"directions informed by the data (s_j^2 > alpha): {np.sum(s**2 > a_mor)} of {n}")
print(f"posterior s.d. along v_1, v_20, v_100: {post_sd[0]:.1e}, {post_sd[19]:.1e}, {post_sd[99]:.1e}")
```

::: ex
[Code 2.13 — What the code shows]{.tag} Least squares is destroyed by noise amplification (Example 2.5).

-   Tikhonov with the discrepancy principle picks $\alpha = 3.5 \cdot 10^{-4}$ and a relative error of 0.186, close to the oracle value 0.176 obtained with the unknown truth.
-   TSVD with 10, 20 and 40 terms gives 0.368, 0.238 and 0.199.
-   In the Bayesian reading, only 31 of the 200 directions are informed by the data. The posterior standard deviation is $10^{-3}$ along $v_1$ and equals the prior value 0.053 along $v_{100}$.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Least squares is the minimum-norm solution of the normal equations, and the best linear unbiased estimator (Theorems 2.1 and 2.2).
-   Its error along $v_j$ has variance $\sigma^2 / s_j^2$: small singular values amplify noise without bound (Proposition 2.4).
-   Spectral filters trade bias for variance (Theorem 2.8); the discrepancy principle chooses the trade-off from the noise level (Proposition 2.9).
-   A Gaussian prior turns least squares into Tikhonov regularisation with $\alpha = \sigma^2/\gamma^2$, and gives a posterior covariance for free (Theorem 2.10, Corollary 2.11).
:::

## 3. Time-reversal imaging {#ch3}

The first application of ch. 2 is imaging itself. Least squares on a fine grid of pixels is hopelessly ill posed; its strongly regularised limit, back-propagation of the time-reversed data, is stable, and its resolution can be computed exactly. This chapter derives migration from ch. 2, explains physical time reversal through the Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity, and ends with the subspace methods DORT and MUSIC.

### Migration as strongly regularised least squares

Fix a search grid $z_1, \dots, z_P$ of candidate positions with unknown reflectivities $\rho \in \mathbb{C}^P$. By Proposition 1.7 the data depend linearly on $\rho$:
$$
\mathcal{K} \rho = k^2 \sum_{p=1}^P \rho_p\, g(z_p)\, g(z_p)^\top \in \mathbb{C}^{N \times N} .
$$

With the Frobenius inner product on matrices, the adjoint is
$$
(\mathcal{K}^* A)_p = k^2\, g(z_p)^*\, A\, \overline{g(z_p)} .
$$

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Kirchhoff migration]{.tag} The Kirchhoff migration (KM) imaging function of a response matrix $A$ is
$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{KM}}(z) = g(z)^*\, A\, \overline{g(z)} = \sum_{n, m = 1}^N \overline{\hat G(x_n, z)}\; A_{nm}\; \overline{\hat G(z, x_m)} .
$$

With several frequencies, the images are summed over $\omega$. Conjugation is time reversal in the Fourier domain: the data are sent back into the medium, from the receivers and from the sources, and evaluated at $z$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Migration is the limit of Tikhonov regularisation]{.tag} Let $\rho_\alpha$ be the Tikhonov solution of $\mathcal{K}\rho = A$. Then, as $\alpha \to \infty$,
$$
\alpha\, \rho_\alpha \longrightarrow \mathcal{K}^* A, \qquad \text{that is,} \qquad \alpha\, (\rho_\alpha)_p \to k^2\, \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{KM}}(z_p) .
$$

::: proof
By Proposition 2.7,
$$
\alpha\, \rho_\alpha = \big(I + \mathcal{K}^* \mathcal{K} / \alpha\big)^{-1} \mathcal{K}^* A ,
$$
and the matrix in front tends to the identity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Migration is therefore least squares with so much regularisation that only the adjoint survives. By Theorem 2.8 its variance is under control; its bias is a blur, since the image of the exact data is $\mathcal{K}^* \mathcal{K} \rho$. The blur kernel is the point spread function computed below.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Delay and sum]{.tag} In three dimensions, integrate the migration of the data over all frequencies with the measure $d\omega / 2\pi$. The result is a sum of the time-domain data at the round-trip travel times:
$$
\int \sum_{n, m} \overline{\hat G(x_n, z)}\, \hat A_{nm}(\omega)\, \overline{\hat G(z, x_m)}\, \frac{d\omega}{2\pi} = \sum_{n, m} \frac{A_{nm}\big(T(x_n, z) + T(z, x_m)\big)}{16\pi^2\, |x_n - z|\, |z - x_m|} .
$$

::: proof
By Proposition 1.4, the product of the two conjugate Green's functions is $e^{-i\omega (T(x_n, z) + T(z, x_m))}$ divided by the two distances and $16\pi^2$. The frequency integral is then the inverse Fourier transform of $\hat A_{nm}$ evaluated at the round-trip time. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This delay-and-sum formula, with $T(x, z) = |x - z|/c_0$, is the beamforming used in ultrasound scanners and the Kirchhoff migration of seismology.

### The time-reversal experiment

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Time-reversal mirror]{.tag} A point source at $y$ emits a pulse $f(t)$. The array records the signals at $x_1, \dots, x_N$, reverses them in time, and re-emits them. In the Fourier domain the re-emitted field at a point $x$ is, up to a phase,
$$
\hat u_{\mathrm{TR}}(\omega, x) = \overline{\hat f(\omega)} \sum_{n=1}^N \hat G(\omega, x, x_n)\, \overline{\hat G(\omega, x_n, y)} .
$$
:::

Experiments by Fink and coworkers show that the re-emitted wave refocuses on the source. The next theorem explains why, and how sharp the focus is.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.5 — Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity]{.tag} Let $B$ be a smooth bounded domain containing $x$ and $y$, with outward normal $\nu$. Then
$$
\int_{\partial B} \Big[\overline{\hat G(x, \xi)}\; \partial_\nu \hat G(y, \xi) - \hat G(y, \xi)\; \partial_\nu \overline{\hat G(x, \xi)}\Big]\, d\sigma(\xi) = 2i\, \mathrm{Im}\, \hat G(x, y) .
$$

For the sphere of radius $R$ centred at the origin, as $R \to \infty$:

::: key
[Key result — Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity, large sphere]{.tag}
$$
\int_{|\xi| = R} \overline{\hat G(x, \xi)}\, \hat G(y, \xi)\, d\sigma(\xi) \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{k}\, \mathrm{Im}\, \hat G(x, y) .
$$
:::

::: proof
Let $u = \hat G(\cdot, y)$ and $v = \overline{\hat G(\cdot, x)}$. Since $k$ is real, $\Delta u + k^2 u = -\delta_y$ and $\Delta v + k^2 v = -\delta_x$.

Green's second identity on $B$ gives
$$
\int_{\partial B} (v\, \partial_\nu u - u\, \partial_\nu v)\, d\sigma = \int_B (v \Delta u - u \Delta v) = -v(y) + u(x) .
$$

By reciprocity, the right-hand side is $\hat G(x, y) - \overline{\hat G(x, y)}$, which is the first identity.

On a large sphere, the radiation condition gives $\partial_\nu \hat G(y, \xi) = ik \hat G(y, \xi) + O(R^{-2})$, and the conjugate relation for $v$. The integrand becomes $2ik\, v u$ plus a term of order $R^{-3}$, integrated over an area of order $R^2$; dividing by $2ik$ concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 3.6 — Refocusing and the diffraction limit]{.tag} If the mirror densely covers a large sphere around the source, the time-reversed field is proportional to $\mathrm{Im}\, \hat G(\omega, x, y)$. In three dimensions,
$$
\mathrm{Im}\, \hat G(\omega, x, y) = \frac{\sin(k |x - y|)}{4\pi |x - y|} ,
$$
a focal spot centred at the source whose first zero is at distance $\lambda / 2$.

::: proof
Replace the sum over the sensors by an integral over the sphere in Definition 3.4, use reciprocity, and apply Theorem 3.5. The formula for the imaginary part follows from Proposition 1.4. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The focal spot cannot be smaller than half a wavelength, whatever the mirror: this is the diffraction limit. In the time domain, $\mathrm{Im}\, \hat G$ corresponds to $G(t) - G(-t)$, a wave converging on the source and then diverging from it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.7 — Resolution with a finite array]{.tag} In two dimensions, let a linear array of aperture $a$ face a source at distance $L$, in the paraxial regime $a \ll L$. Along the cross-range direction, the time-reversed field is proportional to a sinc function, with first zero at the Rayleigh distance
$$
\Delta_{\text{cross}} = \frac{\lambda L}{a} .
$$

Along the range direction, with bandwidth $B$, the first zero is at $c_0 / B$ for time reversal of a source, and at $c_0 / (2B)$ for echoes, whose travel time is doubled.

::: proof
Place the sensors at $(s, 0)$ with $|s| \leq a/2$, the source at $y = (0, L)$ and the observation point at $x = (\xi, L)$. The paraxial expansion of the distances gives
$$
|x - (s, 0)| - |y - (s, 0)| \approx \frac{(s - \xi)^2 - s^2}{2L} = \frac{\xi^2 - 2 s \xi}{2L} .
$$

The amplitudes are nearly equal, so a dense array sums the phases:
$$
\int_{-a/2}^{a/2} e^{-i k s \xi / L}\, ds = a\, \frac{\sin(k a \xi / 2L)}{k a \xi / 2L} ,
$$
which vanishes first when $k a \xi / 2L = \pi$, that is, $\xi = \lambda L / a$.

Along the range, a shift $\eta$ changes the phase by $k\eta$ for a source and by $2k\eta$ for an echo.

Integrating over a band of width $2\pi B$ around $\omega_0$ gives a sinc in $\pi B \eta / c_0$ or in $2\pi B \eta / c_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Stability: the signal-to-noise ratio of migration

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.8 — Migration gains a factor N]{.tag} Let $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = k^2 \rho\, g g^\top + W$, with $g = g(z_1)$ and $W$ as in Definition 1.8. At the reflector,
$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{KM}}(z_1) = \rho\, k^2 \|g\|^4 + \|g\|^2\, Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2) ,
$$
so the signal-to-noise ratio of the image is $|\rho|\, k^2 \|g\|^2 / \sigma$.

When the moduli of the $g_n$ are comparable, this is $N$ times the signal-to-noise ratio of a single entry. With $F$ independent frequencies the gain is multiplied by $\sqrt F$.

::: proof
The signal part is $\rho k^2 (g^* g)(g^\top \bar g) = \rho k^2 \|g\|^4$. The noise part is $\|g\|^2$ times $\hat g^* W \bar{\hat g}$, with $\hat g = g / \|g\|$ a unit vector, which is $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ by Proposition 0.7.

A single entry has signal modulus $|\rho| k^2 |g_n| |g_m| \approx |\rho| k^2 \|g\|^2 / N$ and noise $\sigma$. Over $F$ frequencies the signals add coherently and the independent noises add in variance. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.9 — Resolution and stability by numbers]{.tag}

-   In echography with $\lambda = 0.31$ mm, an aperture $a = 4$ cm, a depth $L = 6$ cm and a bandwidth of 3 MHz, the cross-range resolution is $0.46$ mm and the range resolution of echoes is $1540 / (6 \cdot 10^6)$ m, about $0.26$ mm.
-   In Code 1.10 the first reflector gives $|\rho| k^2 \|g\|^2 \approx 0.335$ and $\sigma = 0.01$. The image signal-to-noise ratio at the reflector is about 34, while each entry of the data has a ratio close to 1.
:::

### Iterative time reversal, DORT and MUSIC

Re-emitting the conjugate of the recorded field twice maps an input $v$ to $\bar A A v = A^* A v$, since $A$ is symmetric. Iterating time reversal is thus the power method on the time-reversal operator $A^* A$: it converges to the top singular vector, and the array focuses on the strongest reflector. The DORT method of Prada and Fink uses all the singular vectors at once.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.10 — Well-separated reflectors]{.tag} If the normalised illumination vectors $\hat g_r = g(z_r)/\|g(z_r)\|$ are orthonormal, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are
$$
\sigma_r = |\rho_r|\, k^2\, \|g(z_r)\|^2, \qquad r = 1, \dots, R,
$$
with left singular vectors $\hat g_r$ and right singular vectors $\overline{\hat g_r}$, up to phases. Back-propagating the $r$-th singular vector focuses on $z_r$ alone.

::: proof
Write
$$
A = \sum_r \rho_r k^2 \|g(z_r)\|^2\, \hat g_r\, \overline{\hat g_r}^{\,*} .
$$

Both families $(\hat g_r)$ and $(\overline{\hat g_r})$ are orthonormal, so this is a singular value decomposition once the phases of the $\rho_r$ are absorbed. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Orthogonality holds approximately when the reflectors are farther apart than the Rayleigh distance of Proposition 3.7. Closer reflectors mix their singular vectors, but not their signal subspace, which MUSIC exploits.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.11 — MUSIC characterisation]{.tag} Let $R < N$, and assume that the illumination vectors of any $R + 1$ distinct points of the search region are linearly independent. Let $P_\perp$ be the orthogonal projection onto the orthogonal of the range of $A$. For $z$ in the search region,
$$
P_\perp\, g(z) = 0 \iff z \in \{z_1, \dots, z_R\} .
$$

The MUSIC imaging function is therefore infinite exactly at the reflectors:
$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{MU}}(z) = \|P_\perp \hat g(z)\|^{-2} .
$$

::: proof
Write $A = \mathbf{G} D \mathbf{G}^\top$ with $\mathbf{G} = [g(z_1), \dots, g(z_R)]$ and $D$ diagonal invertible.

The matrix $\mathbf{G}$ has rank $R$, so $\mathbf{G}^\top$ maps onto $\mathbb{C}^R$, and the range of $A$ is the span of the $g(z_r)$.

That span contains $g(z_r)$, which proves one direction. If it contained $g(z)$ for another $z$, the $R + 1$ vectors would be linearly dependent, which is excluded. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With noisy data, the range is replaced by the span of the $R$ leading left singular vectors. This needs an estimate of $R$, which ch. 5 obtains from random matrix theory.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.special import hankel1

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N = 41
xs = np.stack([(np.arange(N) - 20) * 0.5, np.zeros(N)], axis=1)   # aperture a = 20 (wavelengths)
refl = [(np.array([-2.0, 30.0]), 1.0), (np.array([3.0, 32.0]), 0.6)]
ks = 2 * np.pi * np.linspace(0.8, 1.2, 21)                         # band B = 0.4, centre lambda = 1
sigma = 0.01

def g(k, z):                     # illumination vectors, z of shape (..., 2) -> (..., N)
    r = np.linalg.norm(z[..., None, :] - xs, axis=-1)
    return 0.25j * hankel1(0, k * r)

def msr(k):                      # Born response matrix + measurement noise
    A = sum(rho * k**2 * np.outer(g(k, z), g(k, z)) for z, rho in refl)
    return A + sigma * (rng.standard_normal((N, N)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((N, N))) / np.sqrt(2)

data = [msr(k) for k in ks]
X, Y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(-6, 7.01, 0.1), np.arange(26, 36.01, 0.1))
Z = np.stack([X, Y], axis=-1)

def kirchhoff(freqs):            # I(z) = sum_k g(z)^* A_k conj(g(z))
    I = 0
    for i in freqs:
        G = g(ks[i], Z)
        I = I + np.einsum("...n,nm,...m->...", G.conj(), data[i], G.conj())
    return np.abs(I)

I_multi = kirchhoff(range(len(ks)))
iy, ix = np.unravel_index(I_multi.argmax(), I_multi.shape)
print(f"migration peak at ({X[iy, ix]:.1f}, {Y[iy, ix]:.1f})")

# cross-range and range profiles through the first reflector
I_one = kirchhoff([10])                                   # centre frequency only
row = I_one[np.argmin(np.abs(Y[:, 0] - 30.0))]
xr = X[0]; j0 = np.argmin(np.abs(xr + 2.0))
first_null = xr[j0 + np.argmax(np.diff(row[j0:]) > 0)] + 2.0
print(f"cross-range first null at {first_null:.1f} (Rayleigh lambda L / a = {30 / 20:.1f})")
col = I_multi[:, np.argmin(np.abs(xr + 2.0))]
y0 = np.argmin(np.abs(Y[:, 0] - 30.0))
print(f"range first null at {Y[y0 + np.argmax(np.diff(col[y0:]) > 0), 0] - 30:.1f} (c / 2B = {1 / (2 * 0.4):.2f})")

# MUSIC at the centre frequency, signal space of dimension 2
U = np.linalg.svd(data[10])[0][:, :2]
G = g(ks[10], Z); G /= np.linalg.norm(G, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
proj = np.linalg.norm(G - (G @ U.conj()) @ U.T, axis=-1)
music = 1 / proj**2
for half in [X < 0.5, X >= 0.5]:                    # one search window per half-plane
    m = np.where(half, music, 0)
    iy, ix = np.unravel_index(m.argmax(), m.shape)
    print(f"MUSIC peak at ({X[iy, ix]:.1f}, {Y[iy, ix]:.1f})")
```

::: ex
[Code 3.12 — What the code shows]{.tag} The geometry of Code 1.10 is probed at 21 frequencies with a relative bandwidth of 40 %, and imaged on a grid of step $\lambda / 10$.

-   The migration image peaks at $(-2.0, 30.0)$, exactly at the first reflector.
-   Its first zero is at 1.4 wavelengths in cross-range, against $\lambda L / a = 1.5$, and at 1.2 in range, against $c_0 / 2B = 1.25$ (Proposition 3.7).
-   MUSIC with $R = 2$ at the central frequency finds both reflectors, at $(-2.0, 29.9)$ and $(3.0, 32.1)$, although each entry of the data is as noisy as it is informative.
:::

In a randomly scattering medium, physical time reversal refocuses even better than in a homogeneous one: multiple scattering widens the effective aperture, and the refocused field is statistically stable (Fink, 1997; Blomgren, Papanicolaou and Zhao, 2002). Migration of the recorded data, by contrast, is blurred by clutter; ch. 8 returns to this contrast.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Kirchhoff migration is the adjoint of the linearised forward map, and the limit of Tikhonov regularisation as $\alpha \to \infty$ (Proposition 3.2); in the time domain it is delay and sum (Proposition 3.3).
-   The Helmholtz–Kirchhoff identity makes time reversal refocus, with a focal spot of half a wavelength (Theorem 3.5, Corollary 3.6).
-   A finite array resolves $\lambda L / a$ in cross-range and $c_0 / B$ or $c_0 / 2B$ in range (Proposition 3.7).
-   Migration multiplies the signal-to-noise ratio of single entries by $N$ (Proposition 3.8).
-   DORT reads reflectors from singular vectors, and MUSIC from the signal subspace (Proposition 3.10, Theorem 3.11).
:::

## 4. Random matrix theory {#ch4}

Ch. 1 and ch. 3 showed that a few singular values of a noisy response matrix stand out of a noise bulk. To turn this observation into a detection test, one needs the law of the singular values of a pure-noise matrix, and the exact way a weak signal emerges from it. Random matrix theory provides both, in the limit of many sensors.

Throughout, $W$ is an $N \times N$ matrix with independent entries of mean zero and variance one, and $X = W / \sqrt N$.

### The Marchenko–Pastur law

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Empirical spectral distribution]{.tag} The empirical distribution of the squared singular values of $X$ is the probability measure
$$
\mu_X = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N \delta_{\sigma_j(X)^2} .
$$

Its $k$-th moment is the normalised trace $\frac1N \mathrm{tr}\, (X X^*)^k$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Marchenko–Pastur, square case]{.tag} If the entries of $W$ have finite moments of all orders, $\mu_X$ converges almost surely, as $N \to \infty$, to the law of density
$$
p(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x (4 - x)}}{2\pi x}, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 4 .
$$

Equivalently, the singular values follow the quarter-circle law of density $\sqrt{4 - s^2} / \pi$ on $[0, 2]$.

For an $N \times M$ matrix normalised by $\sqrt M$, with $N / M \to c \leq 1$, the limit has density
$$
\frac{\sqrt{(b - x)(x - a)}}{2\pi c x} \quad \text{on } [a, b], \qquad a = (1 - \sqrt c)^2, \quad b = (1 + \sqrt c)^2 .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch by the moment method, square case.*

1.  The moments of $p$ are the Catalan numbers $C_k = \binom{2k}{k} / (k+1)$: with $x = s^2$ they become even moments of the semicircle law, a classical computation.
2.  Expand the trace as a sum over closed paths $i_1 \to j_1 \to i_2 \to \dots \to i_1$ of length $2k$ alternating between row and column indices:
    $$
    \frac{1}{N}\, \mathbb{E}\, \mathrm{tr}\, (X X^*)^k = \frac{1}{N^{k+1}} \sum_{\text{paths}} \mathbb{E}\big[W_{i_1 j_1} \overline{W_{i_2 j_1}}\, W_{i_2 j_2} \cdots \overline{W_{i_1 j_k}}\big] .
    $$
3.  Entries have mean zero, so every edge of a contributing path is used at least twice. Such a path has at most $k$ distinct edges, hence at most $k + 1$ distinct vertices, and at most of order $N^{k+1}$ labellings.
4.  The paths that reach $k + 1$ vertices use each edge exactly twice and trace a tree. They are counted by the Catalan number $C_k$, and each contributes $(\mathbb{E}|W_{ij}|^2)^k = 1$; all other paths contribute $O(1/N)$.
5.  The variance of the normalised trace is $O(N^{-2})$, which gives almost sure convergence by the Borel–Cantelli lemma. A law with compact support is determined by its moments. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The bulk of noise singular values thus fills $[0, 2\sqrt N]$ for $W$ itself, with the quarter-circle profile. No noise direction is privileged, by the unitary invariance of Proposition 0.7.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — The edge and its fluctuations]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.2, the largest singular value of $X$ converges almost surely to 2.

For complex Gaussian entries, its fluctuations are of order $N^{-2/3}$ and follow the Tracy–Widom law $\mathrm{TW}_2$:
$$
\sigma_1(W) \approx 2\sqrt N + 2^{-2/3}\, N^{-1/6}\, \mathrm{TW}_2 .
$$

The law $\mathrm{TW}_2$ has mean $-1.771$, standard deviation $0.902$ and 95 % quantile about $-0.23$. Real Gaussian entries give $\mathrm{TW}_1$ instead.
:::

The convergence of the largest singular value is due to Geman (1980) and Yin, Bai and Krishnaiah (1988). The Tracy–Widom limit for the largest eigenvalue of $W W^*$ is due to Johansson (2000) in the complex case and Johnstone (2001) in the real case; the formula above follows by taking a square root.

### The spiked model and the BBP transition

A reflector adds a rank-one matrix to the noise. The question is whether its singular value separates from the bulk.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Phase transition of the top singular value]{.tag} Let $X = \theta\, u v^* + W / \sqrt N$, with deterministic unit vectors $u, v$, a strength $\theta > 0$, and $W$ with independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, 1)$ entries. As $N \to \infty$, almost surely:

::: key
[Key result — BBP transition, square case]{.tag}
$$
\sigma_1(X) \longrightarrow \begin{cases} \theta + \dfrac{1}{\theta} & \text{if } \theta > 1, \\[2mm] 2 & \text{if } \theta \leq 1, \end{cases} \qquad |u^* \hat u_1|^2 \longrightarrow \Big(1 - \frac{1}{\theta^2}\Big)_+ ,
$$
:::

where $\hat u_1$ is the top left singular vector of $X$; the same limit holds for $|v^* \hat v_1|^2$.

::: proof
*Sketch, following Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi (2012).* Write $Y = W/\sqrt N$ and let $s > 2$ be a singular value of $X$ that is not one of $Y$, with singular vectors $x, y$.

1.  The equations $Xy = s x$ and $X^* x = s y$ read
    $$
    \begin{pmatrix} s I & -Y \\ -Y^* & s I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \theta \begin{pmatrix} (v^* y)\, u \\ (u^* x)\, v \end{pmatrix} .
    $$
2.  Invert the block matrix. The diagonal blocks of its inverse are $s(s^2 - YY^*)^{-1}$ and $s(s^2 - Y^*Y)^{-1}$; the off-diagonal blocks contain one factor $Y$.
3.  Project on $u$ and on $v$, and set $a = v^* y$ and $b = u^* x$. One gets two linear equations in $(a, b)$ whose coefficients are quadratic forms in the two vectors.
4.  By unitary invariance, the diagonal quadratic forms converge to $s\, G(s^2)$, where $G$ is the Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko–Pastur law (Lemma 4.5). The off-diagonal forms, odd in $Y$, tend to zero.
5.  A nonzero solution exists if and only if $\theta\, s\, G(s^2) = 1$. With Lemma 4.5 this reads
    $$
    \frac{s - \sqrt{s^2 - 4}}{2} = \frac{1}{\theta} .
    $$
6.  The left side decreases from 1 to 0 on $(2, \infty)$, so a root exists if and only if $\theta > 1$, and then $s = \theta + 1/\theta$. The overlap follows from the derivative of the same equation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Lemma 4.5 — Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko–Pastur law]{.tag} For $z > 4$,
$$
G(z) = \int_0^4 \frac{p(x)}{z - x}\, dx = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4/z}}{2} .
$$

::: proof
Expand $1/(z - x)$ as a geometric series in $x/z$, valid since $x \leq 4 < z$. By step 1 of Theorem 4.2,
$$
G(z) = \sum_{k \geq 0} \frac{C_k}{z^{k+1}} = \frac{1}{z}\, c\Big(\frac1z\Big) ,
$$
where $c(t) = \sum_k C_k t^k = (1 - \sqrt{1 - 4t})/(2t)$ is the generating function of the Catalan numbers. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Below the threshold $\theta = 1$, the signal is invisible in the spectrum: the top singular value sticks to the edge and its vector is asymptotically orthogonal to $u$. Above it, the singular value separates and is biased upwards by $1/\theta$.

:::: prop
[Corollary 4.6 — Singular values of a noisy MSR matrix]{.tag} Let $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = A + W$, where $A$ has a single nonzero singular value $s_A$ and $W$ has independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ entries. For large $N$,
$$
\sigma_1(A^{\mathrm{meas}}) \approx \begin{cases} s_A + \dfrac{\sigma^2 N}{s_A} & \text{if } s_A > \sigma \sqrt N, \\[2mm] 2 \sigma \sqrt N & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$

::: proof
Divide by $\sigma\sqrt N$ and apply Theorem 4.4 with $\theta = s_A / (\sigma \sqrt N)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a reflector, $s_A = |\rho| k^2 \|g\|^2$ grows like $N$ while the threshold $\sigma\sqrt N$ grows like $\sqrt N$: adding sensors always ends up revealing a fixed reflector.

::: ex
[Example 4.7 — Back to Code 1.10]{.tag} There $\sigma \sqrt N = 0.064$.

-   The first reflector has $s_A = 0.335$, so $\theta = 5.2$ and Corollary 4.6 predicts $0.348$; the observed value is $0.345$.
-   The second has $s_A = 0.188$, so $\theta = 2.9$ and the prediction is $0.209$; the observed $0.194$ is within the fluctuations of order $\sigma$ expected at $N = 41$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
def noise(N):                    # i.i.d. CN(0, 1) entries
    return (rng.standard_normal((N, N)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((N, N))) / np.sqrt(2)

# 1. Quarter-circle law for the singular values of W / sqrt(N)
N = 400
s = np.linalg.svd(noise(N) / np.sqrt(N), compute_uv=False)
grid = np.linspace(0, 2, 2001)
cdf = np.cumsum(np.sqrt(4 - grid**2) / np.pi) * (grid[1] - grid[0])
ks = np.max(np.abs(np.searchsorted(np.sort(s), grid) / N - cdf))
print(f"N={N}: largest singular value {s[0]:.3f} (limit 2), Kolmogorov distance {ks:.3f}")

# 2. Edge fluctuations: sigma_1 ~ 2 sqrt(N) + 2^(-2/3) N^(-1/6) TW2, E[TW2] = -1.771
for N in [50, 200]:
    top = np.array([np.linalg.norm(noise(N), 2) for _ in range(300)])
    pred = 2 * np.sqrt(N) + 2**(-2/3) * N**(-1/6) * (-1.771)
    print(f"N={N}: mean sigma_1 {top.mean():.3f}, Tracy-Widom prediction {pred:.3f}, sd {top.std():.3f}")

# 3. Spiked model X = theta u v^* + W / sqrt(N): BBP transition
N = 400
u = np.ones(N) / np.sqrt(N); v = np.exp(2j * np.pi * rng.random(N)) / np.sqrt(N)
for theta in [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0]:
    Uh, sh, Vh = np.linalg.svd(theta * np.outer(u, v.conj()) + noise(N) / np.sqrt(N))
    s_lim = theta + 1 / theta if theta > 1 else 2.0
    ov_lim = max(1 - 1 / theta**2, 0.0)
    print(f"theta={theta:.1f}: sigma_1={sh[0]:.3f} (limit {s_lim:.3f}), "
          f"|<u,u_hat>|^2={abs(u @ Uh[:, 0].conj())**2:.2f} (limit {ov_lim:.2f})")
```

::: ex
[Code 4.8 — What the code shows]{.tag}

-   For $N = 400$, the singular values of $W/\sqrt N$ are within Kolmogorov distance 0.006 of the quarter-circle law, and the largest is 1.975.
-   Over 300 draws, the mean of $\sigma_1(W)$ is 13.542 for $N = 50$ and 27.826 for $N = 200$; the Tracy–Widom formula gives 13.561 and 27.823. The standard deviations, 0.29 and 0.23, are small compared with the gaps to the signal values.
-   In the spiked model, $\theta = 0.5$ and $\theta = 1$ leave the top singular value at the edge. For $\theta = 1.5$, 2 and 3 it is 2.171, 2.514 and 3.329, against the limits 2.167, 2.5 and 3.333. The overlaps 0.54, 0.73 and 0.89 match $1 - 1/\theta^2$ = 0.56, 0.75 and 0.89.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   The singular values of an $N \times N$ noise matrix with entries of variance $\sigma^2$ fill $[0, 2\sigma\sqrt N]$ with the quarter-circle profile (Theorem 4.2).
-   The largest one sits at the edge, with Tracy–Widom fluctuations of order $N^{-1/6}$ in these units (Theorem 4.3).
-   A rank-one signal of strength $\theta$ in units of $\sigma\sqrt N$ emerges from the bulk if and only if $\theta > 1$, at $\theta + 1/\theta$, with overlap $1 - 1/\theta^2$ (Theorem 4.4).
-   For an MSR matrix, the threshold is $s_A > \sigma\sqrt N$, and the observed singular value overestimates $s_A$ by $\sigma^2 N / s_A$ (Corollary 4.6).
:::

## 5. Detection tests and what follows them {#ch5}

The first imaging question is whether there is anything to image. This chapter builds tests with a prescribed false-alarm rate from the response matrix, computes their power with ch. 4, and then localises and characterises what was detected.

Throughout, $H_0$ says $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = W$ and $H_1$ says $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = A + W$, with $W$ as in Definition 1.8 and $A$ the MSR matrix of one reflector.

### Tests and the Neyman–Pearson lemma

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Test, false alarm, power]{.tag} A test is a function $\phi$ of the data with values in $\{0, 1\}$, where 1 means “declare a target”. Its probability of false alarm and its power (probability of detection) are
$$
P_{\mathrm{FA}} = \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(\phi = 1), \qquad P_{\mathrm{D}} = \mathbb{P}_{H_1}(\phi = 1) .
$$

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) is the curve of $P_{\mathrm{D}}$ against $P_{\mathrm{FA}}$ as the threshold of the test varies.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Neyman–Pearson lemma]{.tag} Let the data have density $p_0$ under $H_0$ and $p_1$ under $H_1$. Assume that the likelihood-ratio test $\phi^\star = \mathbb{1}[p_1 / p_0 > \eta]$ has false-alarm probability $\alpha$.

Then every test $\phi$ with $P_{\mathrm{FA}}(\phi) \leq \alpha$ satisfies
$$
P_{\mathrm{D}}(\phi) \leq P_{\mathrm{D}}(\phi^\star) .
$$

::: proof
By construction, $(\phi^\star - \phi)(p_1 - \eta p_0) \geq 0$ everywhere: where $\phi^\star = 1$ both factors are non-negative, and where $\phi^\star = 0$ both are non-positive. Integrating gives
$$
P_{\mathrm{D}}(\phi^\star) - P_{\mathrm{D}}(\phi) \geq \eta \big(P_{\mathrm{FA}}(\phi^\star) - P_{\mathrm{FA}}(\phi)\big) ,
$$
and the right-hand side is non-negative because $P_{\mathrm{FA}}(\phi) \leq \alpha$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In imaging, $H_1$ contains unknown parameters: the position and the reflectivity. The generalised likelihood-ratio test (GLRT) replaces them by their maximum-likelihood estimates. Under the Gaussian model, minus the log-likelihood is $\|A^{\mathrm{meas}} - A\|_F^2 / \sigma^2$ plus a constant.

### Known position: migration is the matched filter

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — GLRT for a reflector at a known point]{.tag} Let $H_1$ say $A = c\, g g^\top$ with known $g = g(z)$ and unknown $c \in \mathbb{C}$. The GLRT rejects $H_0$ when the migration image at $z$ is large:
$$
\frac{|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{KM}}(z)|^2}{\sigma^2 \|g\|^4} > \ln \frac{1}{\alpha} .
$$

Under $H_0$ the left side is exponential with mean one, so this test has false-alarm probability exactly $\alpha$.

::: proof
As in Theorem 0.5, the minimum of $\|A^{\mathrm{meas}} - c\, g g^\top\|_F^2$ over $c$ equals $\|A^{\mathrm{meas}}\|_F^2$ minus
$$
\frac{|\langle g g^\top, A^{\mathrm{meas}} \rangle_F|^2}{\|g g^\top\|_F^2} = \frac{|g^* A^{\mathrm{meas}}\, \bar g|^2}{\|g\|^4} .
$$

The log-GLR is this quantity divided by $\sigma^2$. Under $H_0$, $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{KM}}(z) = \|g\|^2 Z$ with $Z \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ (Proposition 3.8), and $|Z|^2/\sigma^2$ is exponential with mean one (Proposition 0.7). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Unknown position: the top singular value

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — GLRT for an unknown rank-one signal]{.tag} If $H_1$ allows any rank-one matrix $A$, the GLRT statistic is
$$
\max_{\mathrm{rank}(A) \leq 1} \frac{\|A^{\mathrm{meas}}\|_F^2 - \|A^{\mathrm{meas}} - A\|_F^2}{\sigma^2} = \frac{\sigma_1(A^{\mathrm{meas}})^2}{\sigma^2} ,
$$
so the test compares the top singular value with a threshold.

::: proof
This is Theorem 0.5 applied to $A^{\mathrm{meas}}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The test ignores the physics of the illumination vectors, which makes it robust: it also detects targets that are not points, or a model with an inaccurate speed of sound.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Threshold for a prescribed false-alarm rate]{.tag} With complex Gaussian noise of known level $\sigma$, the test $\sigma_1(A^{\mathrm{meas}}) > \tau_\alpha$ has asymptotic false-alarm probability $\alpha$ for
$$
\tau_\alpha = \sigma \big(2 \sqrt N + 2^{-2/3} N^{-1/6}\, q_{1 - \alpha}\big) ,
$$
where $q_{1-\alpha}$ is the quantile of $\mathrm{TW}_2$; for $\alpha = 5\,\%$, $q_{0.95} \approx -0.23$.

::: proof
Under $H_0$, $A^{\mathrm{meas}} = W$; apply Theorem 4.3 to $W / \sigma$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When $\sigma$ is unknown, it is estimated from the bulk, for instance by
$$
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{j \geq 2} \sigma_j(A^{\mathrm{meas}})^2 ,
$$
or by fitting the quarter-circle law of Theorem 4.2 to the empirical singular values. Removing the top value makes the estimate consistent under both hypotheses.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — Asymptotic power]{.tag} Fix $\alpha$ and the strength $\theta = s_A / (\sigma \sqrt N)$ of the reflector. As $N \to \infty$, the power of the top-singular-value test tends to 1 if $\theta > 1$, and to $\alpha$ if $\theta < 1$.

::: proof
If $\theta > 1$, Corollary 4.6 gives $\sigma_1 / (\sigma\sqrt N) \to \theta + 1/\theta > 2$, while $\tau_\alpha / (\sigma \sqrt N) \to 2$.

If $\theta < 1$, the top singular value tends to the edge as under $H_0$ (Theorem 4.4). Below the transition its fluctuations are moreover those of the null case, so the test cannot distinguish the hypotheses. Baik, Ben Arous and Péché (2005) proved this for the closely related spiked covariance model; we admit it for the additive model. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Below the threshold, the top singular value is blind, but the data are not. The energy detector, which uses the whole spectrum, keeps a nontrivial power there.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — Power of the energy detector]{.tag} The test that rejects $H_0$ when $\|A^{\mathrm{meas}}\|_F^2$ exceeds its $(1 - \alpha)$ quantile under $H_0$ has, as $N \to \infty$ with $\theta$ fixed,
$$
P_{\mathrm{D}} \longrightarrow 1 - \Phi\big(z_{1 - \alpha} - \theta^2\big) ,
$$
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function and $z_{1-\alpha}$ its quantile.

::: proof
Under $H_0$, $\|W\|_F^2$ is a sum of $N^2$ independent exponential variables of mean and standard deviation $\sigma^2$. By the central limit theorem it is close to $\mathcal{N}(N^2 \sigma^2, N^2 \sigma^4)$.

Under $H_1$, the statistic is $\|W\|_F^2 + s_A^2 + 2\, \mathrm{Re} \langle A, W \rangle_F$. The shift $s_A^2 = \theta^2 N \sigma^2$ equals $\theta^2$ standard deviations. The cross term has standard deviation $\sqrt 2\, s_A \sigma$, of order $\sqrt N \sigma^2$, which is negligible. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The two tests are complementary: the energy detector never reaches power one at fixed $\theta$, while the top singular value is asymptotically perfect above the threshold. Onatski, Moreira and Hallin (2013) study the best achievable power below it.

### After detection: localisation and characterisation

Once a target is declared, the top singular triplet carries its position and strength.

-   **Localisation.** Image with the top left singular vector, $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{SV}}(z) = |\hat g(z)^* \hat u_1|^2$, or with MUSIC (Theorem 3.11). By Theorem 4.4 the peak value is about $1 - 1/\theta^2$ instead of 1, so localisation degrades smoothly as $\theta$ decreases to 1.
-   **Number of targets.** The number of singular values above $\tau_\alpha$ estimates the rank $R$ needed by MUSIC.
-   **Identification.** Comparing estimated features, such as reflectivity or, for extended targets, polarisation tensors, with a dictionary of known targets turns identification into classification.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.8 — Debiased estimate of the reflectivity]{.tag} If $\sigma_1(A^{\mathrm{meas}}) > 2 \sigma \sqrt N$, the estimator
$$
\hat s_A = \frac{\sigma_1 + \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 - 4 \sigma^2 N}}{2}
$$
inverts Corollary 4.6, and $|\hat\rho| = \hat s_A / (k^2 \|g(\hat z)\|^2)$ estimates the modulus of the reflectivity.

::: proof
The map $s \mapsto s + \sigma^2 N / s$ is increasing on $(\sigma\sqrt N, \infty)$. Solving $s^2 - \sigma_1 s + \sigma^2 N = 0$ and keeping the larger root gives $\hat s_A$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.9 — Thresholds by numbers]{.tag} Take $N = 100$, $\sigma = 1$ and $\alpha = 5\,\%$.

-   The threshold of Proposition 5.5 is $20 - 0.63 \times 0.464 \times 0.23 \approx 19.93$.
-   A reflector with $s_A = 20$ has $\theta = 2$; its singular value is about $20 + 100/20 = 25$, well above the threshold.
-   The raw value overestimates $s_A$ by 25 %; Proposition 5.8 removes this bias.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
N, sigma, n_mc = 100, 1.0, 400
def noise():
    return sigma * (rng.standard_normal((N, N)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((N, N))) / np.sqrt(2)

u = np.exp(2j * np.pi * rng.random(N)) / np.sqrt(N)      # unit "illumination" vector
v = u.conj()                                              # MSR matrices are symmetric: v = conj(u)
stats = {
    "top singular value": lambda M: np.linalg.norm(M, 2),
    "Frobenius energy":   lambda M: np.linalg.norm(M),
    "matched filter":     lambda M: abs(u.conj() @ M @ v),   # known position
}
h0 = {name: np.array([f(noise()) for _ in range(n_mc)]) for name, f in stats.items()}
thr = {name: np.quantile(x, 0.95) for name, x in h0.items()}          # false-alarm rate 5 %
edge = sigma * (2 * np.sqrt(N) + 2**(-2/3) * N**(-1/6) * (-0.232))    # TW2 95 % quantile ~ -0.232
print(f"threshold on sigma_1: simulated {thr['top singular value']:.2f}, Tracy-Widom {edge:.2f}")
for theta in [0.2, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6]:
    s_ref = theta * sigma * np.sqrt(N)                    # singular value of the clean matrix
    A = s_ref * np.outer(u, v.conj())
    pd = {name: np.mean([f(A + noise()) > thr[name] for _ in range(n_mc)]) for name, f in stats.items()}
    print(f"theta={theta}: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {p:.2f}" for k, p in pd.items()))

# characterisation: invert sigma_1 = s + sigma^2 N / s
s_ref = 2.0 * sigma * np.sqrt(N)
s1 = np.linalg.norm(s_ref * np.outer(u, v.conj()) + noise(), 2)
s_hat = (s1 + np.sqrt(s1**2 - 4 * sigma**2 * N)) / 2
print(f"true {s_ref:.1f}, raw sigma_1 {s1:.2f}, debiased {s_hat:.2f}")
```

::: ex
[Code 5.10 — What the code shows]{.tag} The simulated 95 % quantile of $\sigma_1$ under $H_0$ is 19.93, the Tracy–Widom value of Proposition 5.5.

-   At $\theta = 0.8$ the top singular value detects in 16 % of the cases, barely above the 5 % of false alarms, and the energy detector in 23 %.
-   At $\theta = 1.2$ and 1.6 the top singular value reaches 81 % and 100 %, the energy detector only 47 % and 85 %. The asymptotic formula of Proposition 5.7 gives 0.16, 0.42 and 0.82, slightly below these values at $N = 100$.
-   Knowing the position changes everything: the matched filter detects in 74 % of the cases already at $\theta = 0.2$.
-   For $s_A = 20$ the raw singular value is 25.51 and the debiased estimate 20.67.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   The likelihood-ratio test is the most powerful test at a given false-alarm rate (Theorem 5.2); with unknown parameters one uses the GLRT.
-   For a known position, the GLRT is migration, with an exact exponential null law (Proposition 5.3); for an unknown rank-one signal, it is the top singular value (Proposition 5.4).
-   Random matrix theory sets the threshold (Proposition 5.5) and predicts the power: blind detection works if and only if $s_A > \sigma\sqrt N$ (Proposition 5.6).
-   After detection, the top singular vector localises the target and the inverse of the BBP formula estimates its strength (Proposition 5.8).
:::

## 6. Spectral properties of stationary random processes {#ch6}

Sensor noise and ambient noise are random signals whose statistics do not change in time. Their spectral description answers the two questions of ch. 7: what does the correlation of two recordings estimate, and how long must one record for the estimate to be reliable?

### Stationary processes

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Stationary process, covariance]{.tag} A real random process $n(t)$ is stationary (in the wide sense) if it has mean zero, finite variance, and a covariance depending only on the lag:
$$
C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}\big[n(t)\, n(t + \tau)\big] .
$$

Two processes $n_1, n_2$ are jointly stationary if, moreover, their cross-covariance $C_{12}(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[n_1(t)\, n_2(t + \tau)]$ depends only on $\tau$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Properties of a covariance]{.tag} The covariance is even, bounded by its value at zero, and positive definite: for all times $t_1, \dots, t_p$ and real coefficients $a_1, \dots, a_p$,
$$
|C(\tau)| \leq C(0), \qquad \sum_{i, j} a_i a_j\, C(t_j - t_i) \geq 0 .
$$

::: proof
Evenness follows from stationarity by shifting $t$ by $-\tau$, and the bound from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The double sum is the variance of $\sum_i a_i n(t_i)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### The power spectral density

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Wiener–Khinchin]{.tag} Let $C$ be integrable, and let $S(\omega) = \int C(\tau)\, e^{i\omega\tau}\, d\tau$ be its Fourier transform. Then
$$
S(\omega) = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T}\, \mathbb{E}\, \Big| \int_0^T n(t)\, e^{i\omega t}\, dt \Big|^2 \;\geq\; 0 ,
$$
and $C$ is recovered by Fourier inversion (Definition 0.1). The function $S$ is the power spectral density of $n$.

::: proof
Expanding the square and taking the expectation,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \Big| \int_0^T n(t)\, e^{i\omega t} dt \Big|^2 = \int_0^T \!\! \int_0^T C(t - s)\, e^{i\omega (t - s)}\, ds\, dt = \int_{-T}^{T} (T - |\tau|)\, C(\tau)\, e^{i\omega\tau}\, d\tau ,
$$
because the set of pairs $(s, t)$ in the square with $t - s = \tau$ has length $T - |\tau|$.

Dividing by $T$, the integrand converges to $C(\tau) e^{i\omega\tau}$ and is dominated by $|C|$; dominated convergence gives the limit. It is non-negative as a limit of non-negative numbers. The inversion formula is Fourier inversion. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The spectral density says how the variance $C(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int S$ is distributed over frequencies. Conversely, Bochner's theorem states that every continuous positive-definite function is the Fourier transform of a non-negative measure.

::: ex
